PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BASED MEDICINE_:
Overview — Evidence-Based Medicine & Medical Statistics
EBM = integrating the best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values to guide decisions.
Two halves
  • The EBM framework (hierarchy of evidence, study designs, appraisal)
  • The medical statistics (diagnostic-test maths, measures of effect, significance)
Cross-ref: Public Health: screening (Wilson-Jungner + the screening concept lives there; the test maths lives here), the individual screening programmes, safe prescribing (appraising drug evidence).
The Hierarchy of Evidence — the EBM pyramid
Level Study type Strength
1 (top)Systematic reviews + meta-analyses of RCTsStrongest
2Randomised controlled trials (RCTs)
3Cohort studies
4Case-control studies
5Case series / case reports
6 (bottom)Expert opinionWeakest
Higher = less bias, more reliable; systematic review/meta-analysis sits at the top by pooling all relevant studies.
Study Designs
Design Direction Measures Best for
RCTProspective, randomised + controlledRR, ARR, NNTEstablishing causation (gold standard for interventions)
CohortProspective — follow exposed vs unexposed forwardRelative risk (RR), incidenceRisk factors, prognosis (good for common outcomes)
Case-controlRetrospective — cases vs controls, look backOdds ratio (OR)Rare diseases, quick/cheap
Cross-sectionalSnapshot in timePrevalencePrevalence surveys
EcologicalPopulation-level—Hypothesis-generating
Trial structures: parallel (groups run concurrently) vs crossover (each patient gets both treatments sequentially — own control). RR for cohort, OR for case-control is the key pairing.
Diagnostic Test Statistics — the 2×2 table
📷 Image placeholder — Labelled 2×2 grid mapping TP/FP/FN/TN to sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV, showing the row/column each formula reads across.
Disease + Disease −
Test +True Positive (TP)False Positive (FP)
Test −False Negative (FN)True Negative (TN)
Measure Formula Meaning
SensitivityTP / (TP+FN)Of those with disease, proportion testing positive (intrinsic)
SpecificityTN / (TN+FP)Of those without disease, proportion testing negative (intrinsic)
PPVTP / (TP+FP)Of those testing positive, proportion who truly have disease (prevalence-dependent)
NPVTN / (TN+FN)Of those testing negative, proportion truly disease-free (prevalence-dependent)
The two rules: SnNOut — a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules Out disease (good for screening); SpPIn — a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules In disease (good for confirmation).
The prevalence point: sensitivity + specificity are intrinsic (don't change with prevalence); PPV + NPV depend on prevalence — as prevalence falls, PPV falls (more false positives relative to true). This is why screening low-prevalence populations generates many false positives (cross-ref screening harms).
Likelihood ratios (prevalence-independent): LR+ = sens/(1−spec) (>10 = strong rule-in); LR− = (1−sens)/spec (<0.1 = strong rule-out).
Measures of Effect
Measure Meaning
Relative Risk (RR)Risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed; RR >1 = ↑risk, <1 = protective (cohort/RCT)
Odds Ratio (OR)Odds of exposure in cases ÷ controls (case-control; approximates RR for rare disease)
Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR)Control event rate − treatment event rate
Number Needed to Treat (NNT)1 / ARR — patients treated to prevent one outcome (lower = better)
Number Needed to Harm (NNH)1 / absolute risk increase (higher = safer)
Relative Risk Reduction (RRR)Proportional reduction — can look impressive while ARR is tiny (the "spin" to watch)
Statistical Significance & Uncertainty
📷 Image placeholder — Annotated forest plot — pooled diamond, individual study CIs and the line of no effect (RR/OR = 1); intervals crossing the line are non-significant.
Concept Meaning
p-valueProbability the result (or more extreme) occurred by chance if the null were true; <0.05 = "statistically significant" (arbitrary threshold)
Confidence interval (CI)On repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals would contain the true value (usually a 95% CI); narrow = precise; if a 95% CI for RR/OR crosses 1 (or a difference crosses 0) → not significant
Type I error (α)False positive — rejecting a true null (concluding an effect that isn't real)
Type II error (β)False negative — missing a real effect; power = 1−β (↑ by larger sample size)
Null hypothesisThe hypothesis of "no difference/effect"
CI > p-value: a CI conveys both significance and precision/effect size — more informative than p alone.
Bias & Confounding — appraising validity
  • Bias (systematic error): selection bias (incl. healthy-volunteer), information/measurement bias, recall bias (case-control), observer bias (→ blinding), lead-time + length-time bias (screening — cross-ref public health), attrition bias (dropouts)
  • Confounding: a third factor associated with both exposure and outcome distorting the link (e.g. age, smoking) — controlled by randomisation, matching, restriction, multivariable adjustment
  • Reducing bias in RCTs: randomisation (balances confounders), blinding (single/double), allocation concealment, intention-to-treat analysis
The EBM Process
The 5 A's: Ask (form a focused PICO question — Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) → Acquire (search) → Appraise (critically appraise validity — CASP checklists) → Apply (to the patient, with their values) → Assess (evaluate outcome).
Critical appraisal asks: are the results valid (bias/confounding?), important (effect size/CI?), and applicable (to my patient?).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Hierarchy
Systematic review/meta-analysis > RCT > cohort > case-control > case series > expert opinion.
Design → measure
Cohort → RR (prospective, common diseases); case-control → OR (retrospective, rare diseases).
Intrinsic vs prevalence-dependent
Sensitivity/specificity = intrinsic; PPV/NPV = prevalence-dependent (PPV falls as prevalence falls → screening false positives).
SnNOut / SpPIn
Sensitive + Negative → rules Out (screening); Specific + Positive → rules In (confirmation).
NNT
NNT = 1/ARR (lower = better); beware RRR looking impressive with a tiny ARR.
Significance
p <0.05 = significant; 95% CI crossing 1 (RR/OR) = not significant; CI shows precision + effect size.
Errors
Type I = false positive (α); Type II = false negative (β); power = 1−β (↑ with sample size).
Validity
Confounding controlled by randomisation/adjustment; bias reduced by blinding + allocation concealment + ITT.
Process
PICO for question-framing; 5 A's for the EBM process.

Overview — Public Health: Screening, Health Promotion & Determinants
📷 Image placeholder — Newborn blood-spot ('heel prick', day 5) screens for 9 conditions (CF, congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell, PKU/MCADD and other metabolic diseases); NIPE within 72h checks eyes, heart, hips and testes.
Public health concerns the health of populations, not individuals — its tools work at the level of communities and systems rather than one patient.
The three pillars
Prevention & screening · health promotion · the determinants of health — the organising spine is the levels of prevention, into which all three slot.
Cross-ref: EBM & Medical Statistics (sensitivity/specificity/PPV maths), the disease notes with screening programmes (breast, cervical, bowel, AAA, diabetic eye), vaccinations (primary prevention), notifiable diseases.
Levels of Prevention — the framework
Level Aim Examples
PrimordialPrevent the risk factors arisingPopulation policy — sugar tax, clean air, urban planning
PrimaryPrevent disease before it occursVaccination, smoking cessation, health promotion
SecondaryDetect early/pre-symptomatic diseaseScreening (the key example)
TertiaryLimit damage/complications of established diseaseRehabilitation, secondary-prevention drugs (statins post-MI)
The anchor: screening = secondary prevention (catching disease in its latent/early stage).
Screening
Definition: testing asymptomatic people to detect disease (or risk) at an early, more treatable stage. A screen-positive result is not a diagnosis — it triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test.
Wilson-Jungner criteria
Domain Criteria
The conditionImportant health problem; recognisable latent/early stage; natural history understood
The testSuitable, acceptable, sensitive + specific, safe
The treatmentEffective treatment exists; agreed policy on whom to treat; facilities available
The programmeCost-effective; continuous/ongoing (not one-off); benefit outweighs harm

Biases that make screening look better than it is
Bias What it is
Lead-time biasScreening detects disease earlier → survival appears longer, but only because the clock started earlier — death isn't actually delayed
Length-time biasScreening preferentially catches slow-growing (better-prognosis) disease; fast aggressive disease presents symptomatically between screens
OverdiagnosisDetecting disease that would never have caused harm → unnecessary treatment
Selection (healthy-volunteer) biasThose who attend screening are healthier than those who don't
The harms of screening (it's not free): false positives (anxiety, unnecessary invasive tests), false negatives (false reassurance), overdiagnosis/overtreatment. Test statistics → EBM note.
Health Promotion
  • Definition: enabling people to increase control over and improve their health — broader than just giving information
  • Health education vs health promotion: education = providing information/knowledge; promotion = the wider effort including policy, environment, and enabling change
Ottawa Charter — five action areas
Build healthy public policy · create supportive environments · strengthen community action · develop personal skills · reorient health services.
Approaches span individual (advice, brief interventions), community (programmes), and population/policy (legislation, taxation — "nudge").
Determinants of Health
📷 Image placeholder — Inverse care law (Tudor Hart) — the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need of the population served; a high-yield companion to the Marmot gradient.
The core idea: health is determined far more by social, economic, and environmental factors than by healthcare itself — most variation in population health lies outside the clinic.
Dahlgren-Whitehead "rainbow" model (innermost → outermost)
  • Age, sex, genetics (fixed, innermost)
  • Individual lifestyle factors (smoking, diet, exercise)
  • Social + community networks (family, friends, support)
  • Living + working conditions (housing, education, employment, healthcare access, food)
  • General socioeconomic, cultural + environmental conditions (outermost)
  • Social determinants of health (SDOH): the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age — income, education, housing, employment, environment
  • Health inequalities + the social gradient (Marmot): health follows a gradient — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health, stepwise across the whole of society (not just rich vs poor). Marmot's principle: "the causes of the causes"
  • Equality vs equity: equality = everyone gets the same; equity = allocation according to need (the more relevant public-health goal)
Connects to the health-inequalities consideration in the antimicrobial stewardship note.
Population Health Measures
Measure Definition
Life expectancyYears a person can expect to live from birth if conditions stayed the same
Healthy life expectancyYears expected to live in self-assessed good health
Amenable mortalityPremature deaths that adequate healthcare could have prevented
Mortality rateDeaths per year per 100,000 — affected by healthcare, social, economic + environmental factors

Prevention levels
Primary (prevent — vaccines), secondary (screening), tertiary (limit complications); + primordial (risk factors).
Screening = secondary prevention
Screen-positive ≠ diagnosis (→ diagnostic test).
Wilson-Jungner
The condition (important, latent stage), the test (acceptable, sensitive/specific), the treatment (effective, agreed policy), the programme (cost-effective, ongoing).
UK programmes
AAA (men, 65), breast (50–70, 3-yearly), cervical (25–64, HPV-primary), bowel (50–74, FIT, 2-yearly), diabetic eye (≥12).
Screening biases
Lead-time (earlier detection → apparent longer survival), length-time (catches slow-growing disease), overdiagnosis — the "looks better than it is" trio.
Health promotion
Ottawa Charter (5 action areas); promotion > education.
Determinants
Dahlgren-Whitehead rainbow; social determinants > healthcare for outcomes; Marmot social gradient ("causes of the causes"); equity ≠ equality.

Overview — Notifiable Diseases
A public-health framework note, not a disease note: the legal duty to report specified infectious diseases to public health authorities so they can act to protect the population.
The core principle: you notify on clinical suspicion alone — do not wait for laboratory confirmation, as that delays the public-health response.
The three things examined
Who notifies whom · the timing · why (plus recognising which diseases are notifiable).
Cross-ref the individual notifiable conditions in the app: meningococcal disease, infective diarrhoea, viral hepatitis, TB, measles/mumps/rubella, COVID; plus infection control and contact prophylaxis (meningococcal).
The Legal Framework — who, to whom, the law
📷 Image placeholder — No consent needed — notification is a statutory duty overriding confidentiality; the doctor notifies in the public interest even if the patient objects.
  • Who has the duty: the Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) — any GMC-registered doctor — with "reasonable grounds for suspecting" a notifiable disease
  • To whom: the "Proper Officer" of the local authority (in practice, the local UKHSA Health Protection Team)
  • The legal basis: the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 and the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 — a statutory duty, not optional
Parallel laboratory duty: diagnostic labs have a separate statutory duty to report the isolation of specific notifiable organisms (e.g. Neisseria meningitidis from a blood culture). A lab report does NOT remove the doctor's duty to notify on clinical suspicion — the two systems complement each other.
The Timing — urgent vs routine
Urgent cases Routine cases
HowTelephone the HPTOnline / written notification form
WhenWithin 24 hoursWithin 3 days
ExamplesMeningococcal disease, measles, food-poisoning outbreaksTB, mumps, scarlet fever
Urgent cases are phoned within 24 h because there is often a critical window for control measures; all cases (including urgent) also need the written/online form within 3 days.
The golden rule again: notify on clinical suspicion — do not wait for lab confirmation.
The List — grouped to be learnable
📷 Image placeholder — Colour-coded grid of the statutory notifiable diseases vs the classic NON-notifiable traps (MRSA, C. difficile, CJD, HIV).
The full statutory list is ~30+; the realistic expectation is to recognise a disease as notifiable and know the high-yield ones.
Category Diseases
Already in your app (cross-ref)Meningococcal disease/meningitis, acute (incl. bloody) diarrhoea / food poisoning, acute hepatitis (A–E), TB, measles, mumps, rubella, COVID-19, whooping cough
Vaccine-preventable / childhoodMeasles, mumps, rubella, pertussis (whooping cough), diphtheria, tetanus, polio (acute poliomyelitis)
Severe bacterial / toxinMeningococcal septicaemia, scarlet fever, diphtheria, tetanus, anthrax, botulism, plague
GI / food & waterFood poisoning, cholera, typhoid & paratyphoid (enteric fever), infectious bloody diarrhoea, acute hepatitis A/E
Respiratory / environmentalTB, Legionnaires' disease, SARS, COVID-19, invasive group A strep
Zoonotic / imported / tropicalRabies, malaria, viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola etc.), brucellosis, yellow fever, typhus
"Definitely know these" high-yield subset: measles, meningococcal disease, food poisoning, TB, mumps, scarlet fever, COVID-19 — focus on the urgent ones and the common routine ones.
NON-notifiable infections (the classic trap): MRSA / Staph aureus, C. difficile, CJD have separate surveillance, not statutory notification. HIV is also NOT statutorily notifiable (confidential surveillance).
The "All-Hazards" Catch-All Principle — often missed
  • The duty isn't limited to the listed diseases: an RMP should notify any infection or contamination (including non-listed/emerging infections, and chemical/radiation hazards) that presents, or could present, significant harm to human health — e.g. a novel pathogen, a cluster, or carbon monoxide poisoning
  • Example: notifying parvovirus B19 in a contact of a pregnant woman, even though it's not on the formal list
Why Notify — the public-health rationale
  • Surveillance (tracking incidence and trends), outbreak detection, contact tracing, and implementing control measures to prevent further spread
  • Some notifications trigger immediate public-health action — antibiotics, vaccination, or isolation advice for contacts; others strengthen surveillance and let UKHSA assess interventions like vaccine programmes
What Happens After Notification — breaking the chain
  • Contact tracing (identifying and monitoring close contacts)
  • Prophylaxis — vaccination or antibiotics for contacts (e.g. ciprofloxacin for meningococcal contacts)
  • Environmental investigation — water systems for Legionella, premises for food poisoning
The HPT takes over the epidemiological work; the doctor's job is the prompt, suspicion-based notification.
⭐ Exam Pearls
The duty
Falls on the RMP (any GMC-registered doctor), on clinical suspicion — do NOT wait for lab confirmation.
To whom
The "Proper Officer" / local UKHSA Health Protection Team.
Timing
Urgent → phone within 24 h (meningococcal, measles, outbreaks); all → written/online within 3 days.
Lab duty
Labs have a parallel duty to report organisms — doesn't replace the doctor's clinical notification.
High-yield notifiable
Measles, meningococcal, food poisoning, TB, mumps, rubella, whooping cough, COVID, hepatitis, cholera, typhoid, rabies, VHF.
NOT notifiable (the trap)
MRSA, C. difficile, CJD, HIV — separate surveillance systems.
"All-hazards" principle
Notify anything (incl. non-listed/emerging infections, chemical/radiation hazards) that could significantly harm public health.
Purpose
Surveillance + outbreak control + contact tracing + prophylaxis (population protection, not individual treatment).
